steps.body: Two special triangles hand you exact values forever. The half-equilateral (30-60-90) and half-square (45-45-90) give: **sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = √2/2, sin 60° = √3/2** — and cosines run the same list BACKWARD. Memory device: √1/2, √2/2, √3/2 — sine climbs the roots as the angle grows.
Exact values, read off the circle.

widget.prompt: Rotate to 240°. Read the coordinates, and notice which 60° angle it leans on.
widget.successFeedback: 240° lands in the third quadrant, leaning on a 60° reference angle — so cos 240° = −1/2 and sin 240° = −√3/2. Both negative, because the third quadrant is where both coordinates are. The exact values are not memorised; they are the 30-60-90 triangle, placed and signed.
widget.lowFeedback: Not far enough — 240° is past 180° but short of 270°.
widget.highFeedback: Too far round; you have passed 240°.

predict.prompt: You'll rotate from 0° to 240°. What does the point's HEIGHT do along the way?
predict.reveal: The height rises until the top of the circle at 90°, then falls — the sine's peak is exactly where the point is highest.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents tf exact values.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for tf exact values must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines tf exact values.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: cos 45° = √2/2 ≈ 0.71 — at 45° the half-square's legs are equal, so sine and cosine MATCH.
45° is the crossover: below it cosine is larger, above it sine takes over.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.5 is cos 60° — cosine runs the ladder DOWNWARD. At the 45° balance point it equals √2/2 ≈ 0.71.
0.87 is cos 30° — one rung early. At 45° both functions meet at √2/2 ≈ 0.71.

steps.body: Combine the table with reference angles and the WHOLE circle is exact. cos 300°: quadrant IV (the C quadrant — cosine positive), reference 360 − 300 = 60°, magnitude cos 60° = 1/2. So cos 300° = **+0.5**. Reference for size, A-S-T-C for sign, table for the number.

commonErrors.feedback: Quadrant IV is the C quadrant — x > 0 there, so cosine stays POSITIVE: +0.5.
0.87 borrows cos 30° — but 300°'s reference is 60°, and cos 60° = 1/2.

explanationVariants: 330° is Q4 with reference 30°: magnitude sin 30° = 1/2, and Q4's y < 0 flips it: −0.5.
Only cosine survives positive in Q4 — sine dips below.

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right, but 330° sits BELOW the x-axis (Q4) — sine is negative: −0.5.
−0.87 is √3/2's magnitude — that belongs to COS of a 30° reference. Sine of 30° is 1/2: answer −0.5.

steps.body: Radians change nothing but the labels: **sin(π/6) = 1/2, sin(π/4) = √2/2, sin(π/3) = √3/2.** The denominator names the family — 6 for the 30s, 4 for the 45s, 3 for the 60s — and reference-angle rules run in π-form exactly as before.

commonErrors.feedback: π/3 is the 60° family — 1/2 belongs to π/6 (the 30s). sin(π/3) = √3/2 ≈ 0.87.
1.05 is π/3 itself converted to a decimal — the SINE of it is wanted: √3/2 ≈ 0.87.

explanationVariants: 7π/6 = 210°: Q3, reference π/6 (30°), magnitude cos 30° = √3/2 ≈ 0.87 — and Q3 turns cosine negative: −0.87.
Q3 is the T quadrant — both sine and cosine go negative there.

commonErrors.feedback: Magnitude right — but 7π/6 (210°) is Quadrant III, where x < 0: cosine is NEGATIVE, −0.87.
−0.5 grabs sin 30°'s magnitude — cosine of a 30° reference is √3/2 ≈ 0.87. Answer −0.87.

hints: Place it: 7π/6 is one π/6-step past π — Quadrant III.
Q3 sign for cosine is negative — finish.

takeaways: Sines climb √1/2, √2/2, √3/2 across 30-45-60; cosines run it backward.
Any angle: reference for magnitude, A-S-T-C for sign, table for the value.
steps.teaser: Next: set the circle spinning and watch the y-coordinate draw a WAVE.

concept.body: The anchor value of the whole table: sin 30° = 1/2, exactly. It comes from folding an equilateral triangle in half — the side opposite 30° is half the hypotenuse, always. From this one value the ladder climbs: √2/2 at 45°, √3/2 at 60°.

explanationVariants: Half-equilateral: the 30° corner faces a side half the hypotenuse's length.

widget.prompt: What is sin 30°? (Exact: give the decimal.)

commonErrors.feedback: 0.87 is √3/2 — that's sin 60° (or cos 30°). The 30° sine is the ladder's bottom: 1/2.
30 is the angle — its sine is the ratio 1/2.
